category: Formal, legal, Latin, and archaic prepositions

entries.register: business and commercial; widely condemned by usage guides
entries.complement: noun phrase — never a finite clause (✗ as per we agreed; write as per our agreement), never a gerund (✗ as per shipping it Tuesday; write as per the Tuesday shipping date). Before usual it takes no article: as per usual, and the phrase is frozen — you cannot extend the pattern (✗ as per normal, ✗ as per always).
entries.pattern: as per [noun phrase] · [clause], as per [noun phrase] · as per usual (fixed)
entries.contrast: As per adds nothing whatever to bare per, and every American usage guide from Fowler forward calls it commercialese. Prefer per, or better still plain according to or as you requested. The one form nobody objects to is the jocular fixed phrase as per usual, where the redundancy is the joke.
variants: per is the plain replacement, and according to the plainer one
as per usual is the frozen jocular phrase
per usual is the American clipping of it
entries.meaning: A hybrid of English as and Latin per that grew up in nineteenth-century shipping and invoicing correspondence and never got out of it. It is not ungrammatical — only redundant, and dated in a way that makes business prose sound like a telegram. 1. In accordance with; as specified in — the ordinary commercial use. Shipped as per your instructions of the 14th. 2. In the frozen jocular phrase as per usual, "as always." He was twenty minutes late, as per usual.
examples: Shipped as per your instructions of the 14th.
The invoice was prepared as per the terms of the purchase order.
He was twenty minutes late, as per usual.
As per the attached schedule, delivery begins in March.
The specimens were tested as per ASTM D638.
As per our conversation, I have enclosed the revised bid.
As per usual, the meeting ran forty minutes over and settled nothing.

entries.register: legal — pleadings and court filings
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a representative (counsel, guardian, trustee, agent) — never a clause, never a gerund. Always set off by commas inside the party designation.
entries.pattern: [party], by and through [attorney, guardian, or agent], [verb].
entries.contrast: A doublet in which by alone would carry the whole meaning; it survives because it sits in every pleading form book. It points the opposite way from on behalf of: by and through names the agent who does the acting, on behalf of names the principal the acting is done for. The related by his attorney is the older and shorter form still used in some state courts.
variants: by and through her undersigned counsel is the fullest form
by alone is the plain-language replacement
entries.meaning: The standard American pleading formula that introduces the lawyer, guardian, or fiduciary through whom a party appears in court. Open almost any civil complaint filed in the United States and it is in the first line of the body.
examples: Plaintiff, by and through her attorneys, Ramirez & Hale LLP, alleges as follows.
The minor child appears by and through his guardian ad litem.
The estate acts by and through its personal representative.
Defendant, by and through undersigned counsel, moves to dismiss the amended complaint.
The tribe sued by and through its tribal council.
Notice was served by and through the registered agent of record.

entries.ipa: /baɪ ˈɔrdər ʌv/ · weak /baɪ ˈɔrɾər əv/ · fully reduced /baɪ ˈɔrɾɚ ə/ before a consonant
entries.register: official and legal — signage, notices, court orders
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming an authority, normally a title rather than a bare personal name — never a clause, never a gerund (✗ by order of closing the road).
entries.pattern: By order of [authority]. (standing alone as a sign or notice) · [clause] by order of [authority].
entries.contrast: By order of names the issuing authority; pursuant to names the instrument. A parking sign reads By order of the Chief of Police; a brief reads pursuant to Municipal Code § 12-4. Its military cousin by direction of signs correspondence for a commander, and at the direction of is the softer civilian form that reports an instruction without invoking legal force.
variants: by direction of (military correspondence)
by authority of (older signage)
entries.meaning: Attributes a command to the office that issued it, and does so in a form short enough to fit on a placard. Americans meet it far more often on signs and posted notices than in running prose.
examples: NO TRESPASSING — By order of the Chief of Police.
The building was closed by order of the county health department.
By order of the court, all filings in this matter are sealed.
Flags will fly at half-staff through Sunday by order of the governor.
The road remains restricted by order of the Forest Service.
Occupancy is limited to 240 persons by order of the fire marshal.

entries.register: legal
entries.complement: as a preposition, only a party's name, and only in a case title (Ex parte Milligan). Everywhere else in American practice it is an adjective (an ex parte motion) or an adverb (the judge ruled ex parte) and takes no object at all. Never a clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: Ex parte [name of the applying party] (case title) · an ex parte [motion / order / communication] (attributive) · [verb] ex parte (adverbial)
entries.contrast: Latin ex parte is "from a party" — one side only. Its opposite is inter partes, both sides participating, which belongs to the frozen family under inter. Do not confuse it with ex post facto (retroactive, and constitutionally forbidden for criminal statutes) or with the commercial ex of ex works.
variants: Ex p. in older reporters
ex parte is set in italics in most American style manuals but roman in the Bluebook when part of a case name
entries.meaning: Marks a proceeding brought by one side without the other present, or a communication with a judge behind an opponent's back — the second being the thing lawyers are ethically forbidden to do. Americans meet it in the great habeas cases Ex parte Milligan and Ex parte Young, in temporary-restraining-order practice, and in every judicial code of conduct. 1. In a case title: on the application of the party named, with no opponent before the court. Ex parte Quirin remains the leading military-commission case. 2. Of a proceeding or an order: heard and decided on one side only. She applied ex parte for emergency custody. 3. Of a communication: made to the judge behind the other side's back — the ethically forbidden sense. Counsel is prohibited from any ex parte contact with the court.
examples: The court granted an ex parte temporary restraining order that afternoon.
Counsel is prohibited from any ex parte communication with the presiding judge.
Ex parte Quirin remains the leading military-commission case.
She applied ex parte for emergency custody of the children.
The order was vacated because it had been obtained ex parte.
Patent examiners handle ex parte reexamination without the challenger present.
Ex parte Milligan held that civilians could not be tried by military commission while the civil courts were open.
The judge disclosed the ex parte phone call on the record the next morning.

entries.register: legal — contract drafting
entries.complement: none. This word takes no object. Its object is already inside it: here means "this document," so hereunder is a complete phrase meaning "under this agreement." Writing hereunder this contract is an error, and so is hereunder to Section 4.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] hereunder · [verb phrase] hereunder · rights and obligations hereunder
entries.contrast: Hereunder points at the document you are reading; thereunder points at some other instrument just named. Mixing them up changes what a contract means. The whole family is a preposition welded to a pointing word — hereof, hereto, herein, hereby, hereinafter, hereunder, herewith, hereinabove — and every plain-language drafting manual in America tells you to replace each of them with under this Agreement, to this Agreement, and so on.
variants: under this Agreement is the plain-language replacement
the here- family: hereof, hereto, herein, hereby, herewith, hereinafter
entries.meaning: A fossil of the Old English habit of putting the object first and letting an adverb swallow it. It is the reason contract prose can refer to itself without ever naming itself, and the reason non-lawyers find contracts unreadable.
examples: The Seller's obligations hereunder survive termination of this Agreement.
Any notice given hereunder must be in writing and sent by certified mail.
Payments due hereunder bear interest at six percent from the due date.
Nothing hereunder creates a partnership or joint venture between the parties.
The Licensee's rights hereunder are personal and non-transferable.
Each party shall bear its own costs incurred hereunder.

entries.register: legal in the contract sense; formal general prose in the other
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause (✗ in consideration of he paid the deposit). For a clause you must write in consideration of the fact that, and you should usually write because instead. A verb after of takes the -ing form and nothing else: in consideration of releasing all claims, never ✗ in consideration of to release all claims.
entries.pattern: In consideration of [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] in consideration of [noun phrase] · in consideration of [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Two different words wear the same coat. In contract law consideration is the technical name for the bargained-for exchange, and this phrase introduces it — a promise without consideration is unenforceable, so the words are doing legal work, not decorating. In ordinary formal prose it means "in view of, out of regard for," close to in light of. Keep it clear of out of consideration for, which means "out of politeness toward" and is a different idiom entirely.
variants: for and in consideration of (the fuller conveyancing doublet)
in consideration whereof (older)
entries.meaning: The phrase that opens the operative clause of nearly every American contract and deed, and the hinge on which the enforceability of the whole document turns. 1. Contract law: in exchange for; as the bargained-for price of a promise. In consideration of the sum of ten dollars, Grantor conveys the following tract. 2. General formal prose: in view of; taking account of. The sentence was reduced in consideration of his cooperation.
examples: In consideration of the sum of ten dollars and other good and valuable consideration, Grantor conveys the following described tract.
The release was signed in consideration of a lump-sum severance payment.
In consideration of the mutual covenants set forth herein, the parties agree as follows.
She accepted the easement in consideration of a one-time payment of $4,000.
The sentence was reduced in consideration of his cooperation with the government.
In consideration of her thirty years of service, the board voted her a full pension.
The policy was rewritten in consideration of the flood risk along the coast.
In consideration of releasing all claims against the estate, she received a lump sum of $250,000.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ˈwɪtnəs wɛrˈʌv/ · older *wh-* /ʍɛrˈʌv/ · weak /ɪn ˈwɪtnəs wɛrˈəv/
entries.register: legal — execution and testimonium clauses
entries.complement: none. Whereof already contains its object — it means "of which," pointing back at the document — so the phrase is complete as it stands. It is always followed by a comma and then a full clause, never by a noun phrase (✗ in witness whereof this deed).
entries.pattern: In witness whereof, [the parties have executed this Agreement as of the date first written above].
entries.contrast: The where- family is the third leg of a three-part system: hereunder points at the document you are holding, thereunder at another one just named, and whereof at the thing last mentioned. Its relatives are whereby, wherein, whereas, whereupon, wherefore, whereto. The variant in witness thereof is usually a drafting slip rather than a genuine alternative — thereof points away from the document that is being signed, which is not what the signer means.
variants: in testimony whereof (state seals and notarial certificates)
witness my hand and seal (the shorter American form)
entries.meaning: The testimonium clause — the fixed line that opens the signature block of an American contract, deed, affidavit, or gubernatorial proclamation. It is not a productive preposition at all: it is a fossil you will read a thousand times and never build a new sentence with.
examples: In witness whereof, the parties have executed this Agreement as of the date first written above.
In witness whereof, I have hereunto set my hand and caused the Great Seal of the State of Ohio to be affixed.
In witness whereof, the undersigned has caused this Deed to be executed by its duly authorized officer.
The notary's certificate appeared immediately below the in witness whereof line.
In witness whereof, the Corporation has caused these presents to be signed this 3rd day of April.
Older forms open the clause in testimony whereof rather than in witness whereof.

entries.register: legal — deeds, conveyances, oil-and-gas instruments
entries.complement: noun phrase — never a clause, never a gerund. The object is the thing carved out of the grant, and it must be described with the same precision as the grant itself.
entries.pattern: [granting clause], save and except [noun phrase] · Save and except [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: A doublet in which both halves mean the same thing: save is the native-English member and except the Latin-derived one, paired by the medieval habit of doubling a word with its Romance twin (will and testament, free and clear, give, devise and bequeath). Ordinary writing wants except alone — and note the division of labor between except and except for: bare except subtracts from a word already in the sentence (everyone except Marcia signed), while except for stands outside the whole clause and qualifies it (Except for the roof, the house is sound). Note also that bare save has a second life as a conjunction taking a clause (save that he arrived late); the doublet does not — save and except is a preposition and nothing else. Finally, a save and except clause reserves an interest to the grantor, while an exception to a warranty merely limits what is being warranted — Texas courts have decided a great many cases on that difference.
variants: saving and excepting (the participial form)
less and except (equally common in mineral deeds)
reserving unto Grantor (the reservation, as opposed to exception, wording)
entries.meaning: The reservation formula of American deed drafting, and above all of Texas and Oklahoma oil-and-gas conveyances, where a grantor uses it to keep the minerals while selling the surface. Read one mineral deed and you will meet it in the first paragraph.
examples: Grantor conveys the surface estate, save and except all oil, gas, and other minerals in and under said land.
The lease covers the entire section, save and except forty acres surrounding the homestead.
All fixtures pass with the sale, save and except the walk-in cooler and the display cases.
Save and except the easement described in Exhibit B, the tract is unencumbered.
The assignment transfers every well on the lease, save and except the Jones No. 2.
Grantor conveys all of Lot 7, save and except that portion previously dedicated to the county for road purposes.

entries.register: formal and legal, but fully current in general American English
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause (✗ subject to the board approves it; write subject to the board's approval or subject to approval by the board). The to is a preposition here, not the infinitive marker, so a verb after it must be an -ing form: subject to obtaining a permit, never ✗ subject to obtain a permit — the same trap as look forward to seeing you, object to being questioned, and accustomed to working late. The gerund may carry its own subject in the possessive or objective case: subject to the applicant's posting a bond. Pronoun objects take the objective case: subject to them, never ✗ subject to they.
entries.pattern: Subject to [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] subject to [noun phrase] · [noun] subject to [noun phrase] · subject to [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Stress separates the preposition from the verb it looks like: the preposition and adjective are SUB-ject /ˈsʌbdʒɪkt/, while the verb meaning "to expose someone to something" is sub-JECT /səbˈdʒɛkt/ (they subjected him to a search). Against its neighbors, subject to makes the main event conditional and revocable — the condition can still undo it later — where contingent on and dependent on merely make it conditional up front, and pursuant to makes it authorized. Subject to change and subject to availability are fixed phrases.
variants: contingent on and dependent on are the near equivalents for the conditional sense
subject to change, subject to availability, and subject to approval are fixed phrases
subject thereto is the legal-fossil form that points back at a document already named
entries.meaning: The most productive word in this file and the only one an ordinary American uses without noticing. Three senses run through it, and they shade into one another: a condition, an authority, and an exposure. 1. Conditional on; not final until something else happens. The offer is subject to a satisfactory inspection. 2. Under the authority, jurisdiction, or governance of. Federal contractors are subject to the same disclosure rules. 3. Liable to undergo; prone to. The coast is subject to flooding every spring.
examples: The offer is subject to a satisfactory home inspection.
Subject to shareholder approval, the merger closes in April.
All fares and schedules are subject to change without notice.
Federal contractors are subject to the same disclosure rules as agencies.
The territory remained subject to the crown for another century.
Any amount subject to withholding must be reported on Form 1099.
The coast is subject to flooding every spring.
He has been subject to migraines since childhood.
The permit is granted subject to the applicant posting a bond.
Closing is subject to obtaining a firm commitment from the lender by June 1.

entries.register: legal and regulatory
entries.complement: none — the object is incorporated. There points at a statute, contract, or provision already named, so thereunder means "under that." Thereunder the statute is an error.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] thereunder · [verb phrase] thereunder · the Act and the regulations promulgated thereunder
entries.contrast: Hereunder points at the document you are reading; thereunder points at some other instrument just mentioned. Drafters confuse the two constantly, and the mistake is substantive, not stylistic — it can redirect an entire obligation. The there- family runs thereof, thereto, therein, thereby, thereafter, thereunder, therewith, theretofore, thereupon.
variants: under that Agreement / under the Act are the plain-language replacements
the there- family: thereof, thereto, therein, thereby, therewith
entries.meaning: The pointing twin of hereunder, and the workhorse of American regulatory citation, where the standard formula is the Act and the regulations promulgated thereunder.
examples: The Act and the regulations promulgated thereunder apply to all interstate carriers.
The lease and the rights granted thereunder were assigned in 2019.
Any claim arising thereunder is barred by the statute of limitations.
The trust and the powers conferred thereunder terminate at her death.
He cited the treaty and two decisions rendered thereunder.
Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 promulgated thereunder prohibit securities fraud.

entries.ipa: /ˈʌndər ənd pərˈsuənt tu/ · weak /ˈʌndər ən pərˈsuənt tə/
entries.register: legal
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming an instrument or a source of authority — a statute, an agreement, an order, a section number. Never a clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [clause] under and pursuant to [statute / agreement / order] · Under and pursuant to [instrument], [clause].
entries.contrast: A pure doublet: pursuant to already means "under." It persists because form books carry it, and it is the first phrase struck by every plain-language style guide, including the federal courts' own. Distinguish by order of, which names the issuing authority rather than the instrument, and in accordance with, which claims conformity rather than derivation.
variants: under alone is the plain-language replacement
pursuant to and in accordance with (a longer doublet of the same kind)
entries.meaning: Derives an action from a written authority, twice over. The only reason to know it is that you will read it, not write it.
examples: The sale is made under and pursuant to the terms of the settlement agreement.
Bonds issued under and pursuant to the Indenture rank equally with one another.
The trustee acts under and pursuant to Article VII of the trust instrument.
Notice was given under and pursuant to Section 1692g of the Act.
The property was sold under and pursuant to a decree of foreclosure entered March 4.
Under and pursuant to the authority vested in me by the Constitution, I hereby proclaim...

entries.register: legal
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause (✗ without prejudice to she may appeal; write without prejudice to her right to appeal). The to is a preposition here too, so a verb after it takes -ing: without prejudice to refiling, never ✗ without prejudice to refile.
entries.pattern: Without prejudice to [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] without prejudice to [noun phrase] · dismissed without prejudice (adverbial, no object)
entries.contrast: The bare adverbial without prejudice, with no to, is far commoner and means something narrower: a case dismissed without prejudice can be refiled, one dismissed with prejudice cannot. British practice also uses without prejudice to mark settlement correspondence inadmissible; in an American court that label has no magic effect, and lawyers write for settlement purposes only under Rule 408. Compare the ordinary privative without, which merely subtracts.
variants: without prejudice (adverbial, no object — the commoner form)
without waiving (the same reservation in plainer words)
entries.meaning: Reserves a right instead of surrendering it. It is the drafter's way of saying that doing this now does not cost me that later, and it is why a party can pay under protest, or settle one claim while keeping another alive. 1. Reserving a substantive right that the present act might otherwise waive. Without prejudice to its right to appeal, the company paid the penalty. 2. In litigation: leaving a claim, a defense, or a position free to be raised again later. The case was dismissed without prejudice to refiling in state court.
examples: Without prejudice to its right to appeal, the company paid the assessed penalty.
The case was dismissed without prejudice to refiling in state court.
Without prejudice to the foregoing, Buyer may terminate on ten days' written notice.
She accepted the interim payment without prejudice to her larger claim.
The stipulation is without prejudice to any party's position on the merits.
Counsel appeared without prejudice to the pending jurisdictional objection.
The parties settled the fee dispute without prejudice to litigating the merits in the pending action.

entries.register: legal, academic, and commercial; a bound element, never a free preposition
entries.complement: only the Latin noun the phrase was borrowed with — ad hoc, ad litem, ad valorem, ad interim, ad damnum, ad idem, ad nauseam. It cannot govern an English noun phrase (✗ ad the committee; write to the committee), and it never takes a clause or a gerund.
entries.pattern: an ad hoc [committee / arrangement] · guardian ad litem · ad valorem [tax / duty] · [officer] ad interim · the ad damnum clause
entries.contrast: Latin ad is "to, toward, for the purpose of," and it is the ad- of adjacent, adhere, and administer; English to and for took the whole job, so the free preposition never entered the language. Against pro, the other Latin "for": pro is "on behalf of" — an attorney serves pro bono, for the public good — while ad is "for the purpose of," so a guardian ad litem is appointed for the lawsuit and nothing else. Watch the American stress and vowels: ad hoc is /æd ˈhɑk/ here, not the classical /ɑd ˈhoʊk/.
variants: ad- as a productive English prefix (adjoin, adjunct, advert)
ad hoc has become an ordinary English adjective and adverb and is no longer felt as Latin
ad valorem is the opposite of a specific duty
entries.meaning: Latin "to, toward, for." Like inter and pro it never became a free English preposition and survives only welded to the noun it governs — but the phrases it is welded into are among the commonest Latin tags in American public life. 1. Ad hoc: for this one purpose; improvised, not systematic. The mayor named an ad hoc committee on flooding. 2. Ad litem: for the lawsuit — of a representative appointed for the case alone. The court appointed a guardian ad litem for the child. 3. Ad valorem: according to value — the tax and customs sense. Property taxes are levied ad valorem. 4. Ad interim: for the time being; in the interval. She served as chargé d'affaires ad interim. 5. Frozen phrases of extent: ad damnum, ad nauseam, ad infinitum. The ad damnum clause demanded ten million dollars.
examples: The mayor named an ad hoc committee to study the flooding.
Scheduling is done ad hoc, which is why nobody knows when the truck comes.
The court appointed a guardian ad litem to represent the child's interests.
An administrator ad litem was named because the executor had a conflict.
County property taxes are levied ad valorem on the assessed value.
Congress replaced the specific duty with an ad valorem rate of six percent.
She served as chargé d'affaires ad interim for eight months.
The appointment was ad interim and lapsed when the Senate reconvened.
The complaint's ad damnum clause demanded ten million dollars.
Counsel repeated the point ad nauseam until the judge cut him off.

entries.register: literary or jocular; mildly affected in plain American prose
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a person, a family, a household, or an establishment — a bare personal name (chez Marie), a family name with the article (chez the Bernsteins), a possessive-marked noun phrase (chez his grandparents), or a French pronoun in the fixed forms chez moi, chez nous, chez toi, chez lui, chez elle. Never an English pronoun (✗ chez me; say at my place), never a clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: chez [name] · chez [moi / nous / lui / elle] · chez [family or institution] (extended sense)
entries.contrast: English at plus a possessive does exactly the same work with no accent and no wink: at Marie's. What chez adds is tone. Note the extended jocular sense "in the world of, over at," where the object is a household, a family, or an institution — things are tense chez Wilson — which has no one-word English equivalent.
variants: chez soi ("at one's own home," reflexive)
chez-soi as a noun in French, not borrowed into English
entries.meaning: French for "at the home or establishment of," borrowed whole and never naturalized. Americans meet it on restaurant awnings (Chez Panisse), in society columns, and in the mock-anthropological register of magazine profiles. 1. At the home or place of business of. We're eating chez Marie tonight. 2. In the world of; over at — of a household, a family, or an institution, and always a little arch. Things have been tense chez Wilson since the election.
examples: We're eating chez Marie tonight.
Dinner is at eight, chez nous.
Things have been tense chez Wilson since the election.
He spent the whole summer chez his grandparents outside Lyon.
The recipe came from a cook I met chez Panisse.
Chez the Bernsteins, nobody went to bed before midnight.
Chez the Roosevelts, politics was simply the family business.

entries.register: legal, academic, and accounting; never conversational
entries.complement: in the citation use, a full case or source citation rather than an ordinary noun phrase. In the free use it is an adverb or a noun with no object at all (two justices wrote contra; the pros and contras). Never a clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: Contra [citation]. (a signal introducing disagreeing authority) · a contra [account / entry] (attributive) · pro and contra (adverbial pair)
entries.contrast: Latin contra is the ancestor of English against and of counter-, and it lost to both. In American legal citation it is the strongest negative signal on a scale that runs see → cf. → but see → contra: contra means the cited authority flatly contradicts the proposition. In accounting, a contra account is one that offsets another, as accumulated depreciation offsets an asset. The Nicaraguan Contras took their name from Spanish contrarrevolucionario and have nothing to do with the preposition's ordinary use.
variants: contra- as an English prefix (contraindicate, contraflow, contradistinction)
contra proferentem (construed against the drafter)
entries.meaning: A Latin "against" that survives in three narrow trades and nowhere else. Note that the free-standing form is not a preposition at all but an adverb, since the thing it opposes is already on the page. 1. Citation signal, governing a full citation: the authority cited flatly contradicts the proposition just stated. Contra Smith v. Jones, 410 F.3d 112. 2. Accounting, attributive: offsetting; paired with another account and netted against it. Accumulated depreciation is a contra asset account. 3. Free-standing adverb or noun, with no object at all: on the other side; against. Two judges of the panel wrote contra.
examples: Contra Smith v. Jones, 410 F.3d 112, 118 (9th Cir. 2005).
Accumulated depreciation is a contra asset account.
The doctrine of contra proferentem construes an ambiguity against the party that drafted it.
Two judges of the panel wrote contra, and the majority did not answer them.
Every argument pro was met within the hour by one contra.
The brief cites four cases in support and, contra, none at all.
Allowance for doubtful accounts is a contra account netted against receivables.
Contra Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 90, which the panel never cited.

entries.respell: KUUM (rhyming with room for most Americans); KUM also heard
entries.register: formal or jocular in the compound-noun use; technical in finance; now largely avoided in American English
entries.complement: a single bare noun, normally hyphenated to the noun before it — never a determiner of its own (✗ a bedroom cum a study), never a clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [noun]-cum-[noun] · cum [dividend / rights / coupon] (securities)
entries.contrast: The construction fuses two roles in one object: a kitchen-cum-dining-room is a single room that is both at once, whereas and would list two separate rooms. In securities pricing cum is the exact opposite of ex — a share sold cum dividend carries the coming payment, one sold ex dividend does not. The word is a homograph of a vulgar English term, and that, plainly, is why the compound construction has all but vanished from American writing while surviving in British.
variants: cum laude, magna cum laude, summa cum laude (frozen; not the same construction)
cum grano salis ("with a grain of salt," now always Englished)
entries.meaning: Latin "with, combined with." The living English use is the hyphenated compound noun naming one thing that does two jobs, and it is the only genuinely productive Latin preposition left in the language — productive, but not much used. 1. Combining two roles in one thing. They built a workshop-cum-guest-room over the garage. 2. Securities: carrying the benefit that is about to be detached. The stock traded cum dividend through Thursday.
examples: They converted the garage into a workshop-cum-guest-room.
He served for years as chauffeur-cum-bodyguard.
She runs a bookshop-cum-café on Third Street.
The building is a chapel-cum-concert-hall with terrible acoustics.
The stock traded cum dividend through Thursday and fell on Friday.
Bonds purchased cum coupon settle at the higher price.

entries.register: legal, academic, and journalistic; a bound element inside fixed phrases
entries.complement: only the Latin noun fixed to it — de facto, de jure, de novo, de minimis, de bene esse. It cannot govern an English noun phrase (✗ de the record; write from the record), and it never takes a clause or a gerund. The de of French borrowings (coup de grâce, de rigueur, de trop) is a different word doing a different job and is not this entry.
entries.pattern: de facto [leader / segregation / standard] · de jure [segregation / government] · review de novo · a de minimis [amount / violation]
entries.contrast: The pair to hold onto is de facto against de jure — what is actually the case against what the law says — and the whole American desegregation story turns on it, because Brown struck down de jure segregation and left de facto segregation standing. De novo is not "again" in the loose sense but "from the beginning, giving no weight to what came before," which is why de novo review is the least deferential standard an appellate court applies. De minimis is the front of de minimis non curat lex, "the law does not concern itself with trifles." Against ex, the other Latin word for "from": ex is "out of" a source, de is "down from, concerning."
variants: the English prefix de- (deflate, derail) comes through French and is a different element
de rigueur, de trop, coup de grâce are French, not Latin
de facto is now set roman in most American style guides
entries.meaning: Latin "from, down from, concerning." It never became a free English preposition, but the four phrases it heads are common enough in American law and journalism that a reader meets one of them most weeks. 1. De facto: in fact, whether or not by law. English is the de facto language of air traffic control. 2. De jure: by law; as a matter of legal right. The statute created de jure segregation. 3. De novo: from the beginning, with no deference to the decision below. Questions of law are reviewed de novo. 4. De minimis: too small for the law to take notice of. The court called the shortfall de minimis.
examples: English is the de facto language of international air traffic control.
After the coup he was the de facto head of state for three years.
The statute imposed de jure segregation, and the Court struck it down.
A de jure government may control no territory at all.
Questions of law are reviewed de novo on appeal.
The tax court heard the matter de novo and disregarded the auditor's findings.
The shortfall was de minimis, and the auditors passed over it.
A de minimis violation will not support a private right of action.
The bishop's deposition was taken de bene esse in case he did not live to testify.
Ownership passed de facto long before the deed was ever recorded.

entries.register: commercial, financial, legal, and technical
entries.complement: it depends on the sense. In the shipping and securities senses, a bare noun with no determiner — ex works, ex dividend, never ✗ ex the works. In the provenance sense the object is an ordinary noun phrase and takes its determiner normally — ex the Sackler collection, ex a Distorted Humor mare. In the frozen phrases (ex officio, ex post facto, ex rel.) the noun is Latin and fixed. Never a clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: ex [named delivery point] (shipping) · ex [dividend / rights / coupon] (securities) · ex [source] (provenance and pedigree)
entries.contrast: Latin ex means "out of, from" and gave English exit, export, and the prefix in ex-president. It is the exact opposite of cum in securities pricing. Against plain out of and from, which took over the whole job: ex survives only where a trade has frozen it into a term of art. The noun an ex, meaning a former spouse, is the same word turned into a noun and is not a preposition.
variants: ex- as a productive English prefix (ex-wife, ex-officio, ex-directory)
ex works, ex ship, ex quay, ex warehouse are defined Incoterms
entries.meaning: A Latin "from" that survives in four separate trades, each of which has hardened it into a term with a precise and non-obvious meaning. 1. Shipping: goods taken over by the buyer at the named point, with costs from there on the buyer. The price quoted is ex works, Rotterdam. 2. Securities: without the benefit that has just been detached. The shares go ex dividend on the fifteenth. 3. Provenance and pedigree: out of a named source or dam. A Ming bowl, ex the Sackler collection. 4. Frozen legal and academic phrases. She sits on the committee ex officio.
examples: The price quoted is ex works, Rotterdam; the buyer arranges carriage.
Delivery is ex warehouse, and freight is for the account of the purchaser.
The shares go ex dividend on the fifteenth of the month.
It traded ex rights all week and the price gap confused retail buyers.
A Ming bowl, ex the Sackler collection, sold for four million.
The colt is by Tapit, ex a Distorted Humor mare.
The treasurer serves on every subcommittee ex officio.
The dean sits on the tenure committee ex officio and rarely votes.

entries.register: legal and academic; not a free preposition in English
entries.complement: only the Latin noun that the phrase fixes to it — inter alia, inter se, inter vivos, inter partes. It cannot govern an English noun phrase (✗ inter the parties; write between the parties), and it never takes a clause.
entries.pattern: inter alia · inter se · an inter vivos [trust / gift / transfer] · binding inter partes
entries.contrast: The homograph inter meaning "to bury" is a different word with different stress — the verb is in-TUR /ɪnˈtɜr/ (they interred him on Tuesday), the Latin preposition IN-ter. Against intra: inter- crosses between separate things, intra- stays inside one, and the entire reach of federal power in America has turned on the difference between interstate and intrastate commerce. The living English descendants are the prefix inter- and the preposition between.
variants: inter- as a productive English prefix (interstate, international, interlock)
inter alios ("among other people," as against inter alia, "among other things")
entries.meaning: Latin "between, among." English took the prefix and left the preposition, which now appears only inside a handful of legal tags — but those tags are common enough that any American who reads a court opinion meets inter alia within a page or two. 1. Inter alia: among other things — by far the commonest, and always parenthetical. The complaint alleges, inter alia, breach of fiduciary duty. 2. Inter se: among or between themselves — of the parties' rights against one another rather than against outsiders. The partners' rights inter se are governed by the agreement. 3. Inter vivos: between living persons — of a gift or trust taking effect during life rather than at death. She created an inter vivos trust. 4. Inter partes: between the parties — binding on them and nobody else. The ruling binds the parties inter partes.
examples: The complaint alleges, inter alia, breach of fiduciary duty and unjust enrichment.
The partners' rights inter se are governed by the operating agreement, not by statute.
She created an inter vivos trust rather than leaving the property by will.
The ruling binds the parties inter partes and settles nothing for anyone else.
The statute lists, inter alia, fraud, duress, coercion, and undue influence.
Gifts made inter vivos within three years of death are pulled back into the estate.
Shareholders may restrict transfers inter se without binding anyone outside the agreement.
An inter partes review is adversarial, unlike ex parte reexamination.

entries.register: legal and technical; a prefix in English far more often than a preposition
entries.complement: only the fixed Latin nouns vires and muros. It cannot govern an English noun phrase (✗ intra the company; write within the company), and it never takes a clause or a gerund. Everywhere else in English it is the bound prefix intra-.
entries.pattern: intra vires · intra-[noun] as a prefix (intracompany, intrastate, intravenous, intramural)
entries.contrast: The pair to memorize is intra vires, within the powers granted, against ultra vires, beyond them — and ultra vires is far the commoner of the two in American corporate law, because nobody writes an opinion about an action that was perfectly authorized. Against inter: interstate commerce crosses state lines and intrastate commerce does not. The living English equivalent is within.
variants: intra- as a productive English prefix
ultra vires is the opposite term and much commoner
entries.meaning: Latin "within, inside." It never became a free preposition in English at all; it entered as a prefix and stayed one, and the few prepositional survivals are Latin phrases quoted whole. 1. Intra vires: within the powers granted — the corporate and administrative sense. The board's action was intra vires. 2. As the bound English prefix intra-: inside one body, state, or system. The transaction was intra-group.
examples: The board's action was intra vires and cannot be set aside on that ground.
Debate over whether the bylaw was intra vires consumed the whole afternoon.
The transaction was intra-group and was eliminated on consolidation.
Congress may not reach purely intrastate activity on a commerce theory alone.
The drug is administered intravenously over four hours.
He played intramural hockey for three years without ever leaving campus.
The old charter distinguished the citizens intra muros from the households outside the walls.

entries.type: marginal (a Latin ablative absolute working as an adverbial)
entries.register: legal and academic
entries.complement: none. It takes no object at all. It modifies a whole clause — usually one saying that a rule applies somewhere new — and it is never followed by a noun phrase or a clause of its own. Where a target has to be named, the preposition doing that work is to: applies mutatis mutandis to the Subsidiary.
entries.pattern: [clause], mutatis mutandis. · [rule] applies mutatis mutandis to [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: The nearest English is with the necessary changes made, or the workaday as applicable. Keep it clear of ceteris paribus ("other things being equal"), which holds variables still while you argue, and of pari passu ("on an equal footing"), which ranks claims against one another. It is a preposition only by courtesy, and it is in this file because the reader will meet it filed among prepositions elsewhere.
variants: mutatis mutandis is the only form — mutandis mutatis is an error
entries.meaning: Latin for "the things that must be changed having been changed." It transplants a rule into a new setting and licenses in advance the small substitutions the transplant needs — swap the party names, swap the dates, and the borrowed clause reads correctly.
examples: Article 12 applies mutatis mutandis to each Subsidiary.
The procedure for appeals applies, mutatis mutandis, to petitions for rehearing.
The same argument holds mutatis mutandis for the second experiment.
Sections 3 through 7 are incorporated mutatis mutandis into this Schedule.
What was said of the Senate applies mutatis mutandis to the House.
The rules of the Superior Court govern, mutatis mutandis, proceedings before the magistrate.

entries.register: neutral in the distributive sense; business or formal in the "according to" sense
entries.complement: in the distributive sense, a bare singular count noun with no article — per person, per mile, per year, never per a person. In the "according to" sense, a full noun phrase with a determiner is normal — per the contract, per your email. Never a finite clause (✗ per we discussed; write per our discussion), never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [amount] per [unit] · Per [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] per [noun phrase] · [Latin noun]: per capita, per diem, per se, per stirpes
entries.contrast: The distributive per competes with the indefinite article — sixty miles an hour, twice a week — which is what Americans actually say; per is what the label, the invoice, and the speedometer print. In the "according to" sense it competes with according to and in accordance with and is the shortest of the three, though some readers still hear it as businessese. As per is this same word with a redundant as bolted on. The clipped per usual is an American joke made out of as per usual.
variants: a / an is the everyday spoken equivalent in the distributive sense
p.a. abbreviates per annum on financial documents
entries.meaning: The one Latin preposition that became ordinary English. Four senses, and they sit at very different heights of formality — the first is on every gas pump in the country, the fourth is in the probate code. 1. For each — the distributive sense, and by far the commonest. Tickets are forty dollars per person. 2. According to; on the authority or instruction of. Per your instructions, I canceled the order. 3. By means of — an older commercial sense, now mostly confined to shipping and correspondence. Shipped per certified mail on the third. 4. Inside frozen Latin phrases, where it keeps its original force. Federal spending per capita rose again.
examples: Tickets are forty dollars per person, and children under six are free.
The car gets thirty-four miles per gallon on the highway.
Interest accrues at six percent per year until the note is paid.
Per your instructions, I canceled the standing order.
The report was filed per the court's scheduling order.
The samples were prepared per the manufacturer's protocol.
Shipped per certified mail on the third of the month.
Notice may be given per facsimile or per overnight courier.
He was twenty minutes late, per usual.
Federal spending per capita rose for the fourth straight year.
The estate passes per stirpes to the children of the deceased brother.
The witness fee is fifty dollars per diem plus mileage.

entries.register: formal, financial, and legal
entries.complement: none — annum is already the object of per, so the phrase is complete. It attaches to a rate or an amount that comes before it and cannot govern anything of its own (✗ per annum the loan).
entries.pattern: [rate or amount] per annum · [amount] per annum, [clause] · interest at [rate] per annum
entries.contrast: Ordinary American English says a year or per year; per annum is what the promissory note says, and it is the wording courts look for when they compute post-judgment interest. Its siblings are per diem (a day — which in American usage is also a noun, the daily travel allowance), per mensem (a month, rare), and per capita (a head). Note carefully that per annum means "each year," not "in the first year": six percent per annum on a five-year note is six percent every one of those years.
variants: p.a. is the standard abbreviation on financial documents
per year and a year are the plain equivalents
per diem, per mensem, per capita are the parallel forms
entries.meaning: Fixes a rate to an annual period, in the one register where the difference between an annual rate and a total matters legally. It is a fossil of the same construction that gives per capita and per diem, and like them it takes no object of its own.
examples: The note bears interest at 7.5 percent per annum from the date of default.
Rent escalates three percent per annum over the term of the lease.
The trust distributes forty thousand dollars per annum to each beneficiary.
Judgment shall bear interest at the statutory rate per annum until satisfied.
The endowment spends four percent per annum of a trailing three-year average.
Ground rent of one peppercorn per annum was reserved in the original grant.

entries.register: legal and technical inside fixed phrases; the free word is an adverb or a noun, not a preposition
entries.complement: only the Latin noun that the phrase fixes to it — pro bono, pro rata, pro tempore, pro forma, pro se, pro hac vice. It cannot govern an English noun phrase (✗ pro the plaintiff; write for the plaintiff), and it never takes a clause.
entries.pattern: pro bono · pro rata · pro se · pro tem · the pros and cons (nouns, not prepositions)
entries.contrast: Latin pro means "for, on behalf of, in proportion to" and is the pro- of pronoun and proponent; English for took over its entire job, which is why the free preposition never survived. Against contra, its Latin opposite, and note that the everyday pair is pros and cons, both of them nouns. Watch the American shortenings: pro bono publico is always cut to pro bono, pro tempore to pro tem, and pro hac vice is said proh-hahk-VEE-chay or -VY-see depending on where the speaker went to law school.
variants: pro- as an English prefix (pro-rate, pro-forma as adjectives)
pro tem is the usual clipping of pro tempore
entries.meaning: A Latin "for" that never made it into free English but is preserved intact inside a set of phrases every American lawyer uses daily and every American voter has heard at least once. Six of them carry the whole word. 1. Pro bono (publico): for the public good — of legal work done free. She took the eviction case pro bono. 2. Pro rata: in proportion; share for share. Losses are allocated pro rata. 3. Pro tempore, clipped pro tem: for the time being. The president pro tempore signed the bill. 4. Pro forma: as a matter of form; on assumed rather than historical figures. The company issued pro forma statements. 5. Pro se: on one's own behalf, without a lawyer. He appeared pro se. 6. Pro hac vice: for this occasion only. Counsel was admitted pro hac vice.
examples: She took the eviction case pro bono.
The firm asks fifty pro bono hours a year of every associate.
Losses are allocated pro rata among the members according to capital account.
Unused premium is refunded pro rata if the policy is canceled early.
He appeared pro se and was outmatched from the first motion.
Courts read pro se filings liberally, but the deadlines still apply.
The president pro tempore of the Senate signed the enrolled bill.
She chaired the meeting pro tem while the chair was in surgery.
The company issued pro forma financial statements reflecting the merger.
The vote was pro forma; the outcome had been settled a week earlier.
Out-of-state counsel was admitted pro hac vice for this matter only.
His pro hac vice application was denied because of the earlier sanction.

entries.register: legal and academic; no free use in English
entries.complement: only the Latin noun fixed to it — sine die, sine qua non, sine prole. It cannot take an English noun phrase (✗ sine a date; write without a date), and it never takes a clause.
entries.pattern: adjourn sine die · a sine qua non of [noun phrase] · [name] died sine prole
entries.contrast: Latin sine is "without," and its descendant through French is sans; the plain modern word is without. Do not confuse it with the trigonometric sine /saɪn/, which comes from Latin sinus and is a different word, though the sine in sinecure (from sine cura, "without care") is genuinely this one.
variants: sine qua non takes a plural sine quibus non in strict Latin, never used in English
entries.meaning: Alive in exactly three phrases. Sine die ends a session with no return date fixed, which is what every American hears reported when Congress adjourns. Sine qua non names the condition without which the thing cannot be. Sine prole marks a line that ended childless, in a will or a genealogy. 1. Sine die: with no day fixed for reconvening. The legislature adjourned sine die. 2. Sine qua non: the indispensable condition — the thing without which not. Trust is the sine qua non of the relationship. 3. Sine prole: without issue; childless — in wills and genealogies. The last holder died sine prole.
examples: The legislature adjourned sine die on the thirtieth of May.
Trust is the sine qua non of the attorney-client relationship.
The hearing was continued sine die and never rescheduled.
The baronetcy lapsed when the last holder died sine prole.
Causation is a sine qua non of tort liability, not the whole of it.
The convention rose sine die at four in the morning.
The pedigree records both sons as having died sine prole, and the estate passed to a cousin.

entries.register: legal and academic; a bound element and, far more often, an English prefix
entries.complement: only the Latin noun fixed to it — sub judice, sub silentio, sub nomine, sub rosa, sub modo. It cannot govern an English noun phrase (✗ sub the statute; write under the statute), and it never takes a clause or a gerund. Everywhere else in English it is the bound prefix sub-.
entries.pattern: a matter sub judice · overruled sub silentio · reported sub nom. [case name] · kept sub rosa
entries.contrast: Latin sub is "under," and English under took the entire job — which is why hereunder and thereunder are built on the English word and not on this one. In American citation sub nom. is the workhorse, marking a case that changed names on the way up — as happens whenever a suit against an official in his official capacity is decided under his successor's name. Sub silentio is a term of criticism: it says a court abandoned a holding without admitting it. Sub rosa has escaped law altogether and now just means "in secret." One transatlantic warning: sub judice in Britain names a real reporting restriction that bars comment on a pending case, while in the United States the First Amendment leaves commentators free, so an American who says a matter is sub judice is declining to comment, not citing a rule.
variants: sub- as a productive English prefix (subcontract, sublease, subsidiary)
sub nom. is the standard citation abbreviation
subpoena is sub poena, "under penalty," fused into a single word
entries.meaning: Latin "under." English kept the prefix and kept under, and left the bare preposition to four courtroom and citation tags — one of which, sub rosa, has walked out of the courthouse into ordinary speech. 1. Sub judice: before the court and not yet decided. Counsel would not discuss a matter sub judice. 2. Sub silentio: silently; without saying so — of a holding abandoned unacknowledged. The panel overruled its earlier decision sub silentio. 3. Sub nomine, abbreviated sub nom.: under the name of, in citation. Affirmed sub nom. Carrillo v. Bettendorf. 4. Sub rosa: in secret; off the record. The negotiations were conducted sub rosa.
examples: Counsel declined to comment on a matter sub judice.
The motion is sub judice, and the record remains sealed until it is decided.
The panel overruled its earlier holding sub silentio and never said so.
Two footnotes abandon the doctrine sub silentio.
The district court's ruling was affirmed sub nom. Carrillo v. Bettendorf.
It is reported sub nom. In re Estate of Whitfield.
The negotiations were conducted sub rosa for eleven months.
He kept the arrangement sub rosa even from his own partners.
The bequest was accepted sub modo, subject to the conditions attached to it.

entries.register: legal; a prefix and a stand-alone adjective in English far more often than a preposition
entries.complement: only the fixed Latin noun vires — and, in older writing, petita. It cannot govern an English noun phrase (✗ ultra its powers; write beyond its powers), and it never takes a clause or a gerund. As an English word ultra is either a prefix (ultraviolet) or an adjective meaning "extreme" (an ultra position), and neither of those is a preposition at all.
entries.pattern: an act ultra vires · the ultra vires [doctrine / defense] · ultra-[adjective] as a prefix
entries.contrast: The pair is ultra vires, beyond the powers granted, against intra vires, within them — see intra — and in American corporate and administrative law ultra vires is far the commoner of the two, because nobody writes an opinion about an act that was perfectly authorized. Against beyond, the living English word: beyond is spatial and open-ended, while ultra vires is a verdict. Note also that the modern corporate statutes have largely abolished the ultra vires defense between a company and an outsider, while it stays fully alive against a government agency.
variants: ultra- as a productive English prefix (ultramarine, ultrasound, ultraviolet)
stand-alone ultra meaning "extreme" is English, not Latin
intra vires is the opposite term
entries.meaning: Latin "beyond, on the far side of." It reached English as a prefix and as a one-word adjective, and as a preposition it governs exactly one noun — but that one phrase is the standard American name for an act that exceeded the actor's authority. 1. Ultra vires: beyond the powers granted — the corporate and administrative sense. The board's guarantee was ultra vires. 2. Ultra petita: beyond what was asked — of a court or arbitrator granting more relief than any party sought. The award was vacated as ultra petita.
examples: The board's guarantee was ultra vires and could not be enforced against the company.
The agency's rule was struck down as ultra vires.
Shareholders sued to enjoin the transaction as ultra vires.
Most state statutes have abolished the ultra vires defense in ordinary contract actions.
Whether the ordinance was ultra vires took three days of argument.
An act ultra vires is void, not merely voidable.
The trustees acted ultra vires in pledging the endowment as collateral.
The arbitrator's award was vacated as ultra petita because it granted relief no party had requested.
A tribunal that rewrites the contract for the parties has ruled ultra petita.

entries.register: neutral; formal in legal citation
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause (✗ versus he stayed home; write versus his staying home). Because it coordinates, the two sides should be the same kind of phrase: speed versus accuracy, driving versus flying.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] versus [noun phrase] · [gerund] versus [gerund] · [case name] v. [case name] · [team] vs. [team]
entries.contrast: Three written forms, three habitats. Spelled-out versus belongs to running prose; vs. to sports, science, and everyday shorthand; v. to legal citation — and Americans read v. aloud as "versus," so Brown v. Board is spoken "Brown versus Board," where British lawyers say "and" in civil cases. Against against, which needs no second term to compare; against compared with, which is neutral where versus frames the two terms as rivals.
variants: vs. (general, sporting, scientific)
v. (legal citation; American style keeps the period)
versus spelled out in running prose
entries.meaning: Latin "turned toward, against," from vertere. It is the most thoroughly naturalized Latin preposition in the language after per, and its three senses run from the courtroom out into ordinary speech. 1. Legal citation: one party against another. Brown v. Board of Education was decided in 1954. 2. Contest: one side against another. Michigan vs. Ohio State kicks off at noon. 3. Comparison: one option weighed against another. It is a classic case of speed versus accuracy.
examples: Brown v. Board of Education was decided in 1954.
The docket lists Hernandez versus the City of Tucson for Thursday.
Michigan vs. Ohio State kicks off at noon.
The heavyweight bout is Ali versus Frazier all over again.
It is a classic case of speed versus accuracy.
We are still weighing renting versus buying.
The chart plots unit cost versus production volume.
Twelve percent this quarter versus eight percent last year.

entries.register: formal and official; rare, and now confined to military, diplomatic, and civil-service appointment notices
entries.complement: a proper name or a title naming the predecessor — never a clause, never a gerund. It is always parenthetical, set off by commas, and it never begins a sentence.
entries.pattern: [appointment], vice [name of the person replaced], [reason for the vacancy].
entries.contrast: Two different words are spelled alike. This one is Latin vice, "in the place of," the same element as in vice president, vice chair, viceroy, vice admiral, and vice versa; the moral vice /vaɪs/ — and the workshop tool, which Americans spell vise — are unrelated. Its living English equivalents are in place of and in lieu of, both meaning "replacing." It does not mean "on behalf of": that is on behalf of.
variants: vice- fused as a prefix in vice president, vice chair, viceroy is pronounced VYSS
vice versa /ˌvaɪs ˈvɜrsə/ is the same word and keeps the older one-syllable pronunciation
entries.meaning: Names a successor and the person succeeded, in the one register that still uses it: the Congressional Record, military promotion lists, the Foreign Service register, and the appointments column of an old newspaper.
examples: To be Colonel: Margaret A. Ruiz, vice Colonel J. T. Nash, retired.
Appointed Ambassador to Portugal, vice Mr. Halloran, resigned.
He takes the chair vice Senator Coburn, deceased.
She was named acting director, vice the incumbent, on administrative leave.
The commission seat went to Ellis, vice Barrow, whose term expired in June.
Lieutenant Park assumes command of B Company, vice Captain Doyle, transferred.

entries.register: archaic; surviving in nautical usage, in Southern and Appalachian speech, and inside frozen legal compounds
entries.complement: noun phrase or a pronoun in the objective case (afore me). As a conjunction — a separate job — it takes a full finite clause (afore he comes), and that use is still heard in rural speech; the preposition itself never takes a clause.
entries.pattern: afore [noun phrase] · afore the mast (nautical) · the afore[said / mentioned] [noun] (fused, no longer a preposition)
entries.contrast: It is simply the old form of before — the same root with the prefix a- instead of be-, and nothing but three hundred years between them. At sea it means "toward the bow" and is the live opposite of abaft, which is the one place it is still ordinary technical English. In law it survives only welded into aforesaid, aforementioned, and aforethought, where it is no longer a preposition at all — and malice aforethought sits in the murder statute of every American state.
variants: 'fore is the casual respelling of the same word ('fore the storm hit)
aforesaid, aforementioned, aforethought are the fused legal survivals
entries.meaning: Where an American meets it: hymns and the King James Bible, Twain and Hardy rendering rural speech, a sailing manual, and the charging language of a homicide indictment. 1. Earlier than; before — of time, the ordinary archaic and dialect use. He was gone afore daybreak. 2. Nautical: forward of; toward the bow — the one place it is still live technical English. The galley lies afore the mast.
examples: He was gone afore daybreak.
The galley lies afore the mast.
She had worked the whole field afore noon.
Get the hay in afore the rain.
Afore the war, this was all orchard.
Nothing grew on that bottom land afore the flood.
The crew berthed afore the bulkhead and the officers aft of it.

entries.register: literary; not archaic, but the marked member of its pair
entries.complement: noun phrase — characteristically a mass noun, a plural, or an abstract noun. Never a finite clause (✗ amidst he was speaking; write while he was speaking), and never a bare gerund clause (✗ amidst being questioned) — though a deverbal noun with a determiner is perfectly normal, since it is a noun and not a verb form: amidst the shouting, amidst the fighting. It is a preposition only: unlike o'er it has no adverbial use and must have an object.
entries.pattern: Amidst [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] amidst [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Two contrasts matter here. Against amid: they are one preposition with two spellings, and American English clearly prefers amid, with amidst running several times rarer and reading as deliberately literary; British usage is more evenly split, so amidst in an American paragraph often signals a writer imitating British prose. Against amongst and among: amid takes what you cannot count — amid the wreckage, amid speculation — while among takes countable individuals you are one of, among the guests. The plain spoken equivalent of both is in the middle of.
variants: amid — the ordinary American form, and the one to use
amidst — literary
midst, 'midst, mid — poetic
British writing uses amidst far more freely than American
entries.meaning: Places something inside a surrounding mass or a surrounding condition. The choice between amid and amidst carries no difference of meaning at all — only of register, which is exactly why the choice is worth making deliberately. 1. In the middle of a physical mass of stuff. Amidst the wreckage they found the flight recorder. 2. In the middle of a surrounding condition, noise, or state of affairs — now the commoner of the two. He resigned amidst rumors of a federal inquiry.
examples: The bill passed amidst fierce objections from both parties.
She kept working amidst the noise of the renovation.
Amidst the wreckage they found the flight recorder intact.
He resigned amidst rumors of a federal inquiry.
A single oak stood amidst the stumps.
Amidst all the celebration, no one noticed her leave.

entries.register: literary; in American prose it reads as an affectation
entries.complement: a plural noun phrase, a collective noun, or a mass of individuals — never a singular count noun (✗ amongst the tree), never a clause, never a gerund. Pronoun objects take the objective case: amongst us, never ✗ amongst we. Like among, it is a preposition only — it has no adverbial life and cannot stand without an object, unlike o'er and withal.
entries.pattern: Amongst [plural noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] amongst [plural noun phrase] · divided amongst [plural noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Against among: identical in meaning, and American English prefers among by something like ten to one — amongst is the dominant form in British writing and is one of the surest tells that an American is imitating it. Against between: the schoolroom rule that between takes two and among takes three or more is only half right, because between is correct for any number when the relation is one-to-one and reciprocal (a treaty between the seven signatories), while among views the group as an undifferentiated mass (divided among the heirs). Against amidst, which takes uncountable stuff rather than countable individuals.
variants: among — the ordinary American form
amongst — literary and British
'mongst — poetic
entries.meaning: Puts something inside a plurality of separate individuals, without singling any of them out. The -st is a late accretion of the same kind that produced whilst and amidst, and it never carried any extra meaning. 1. In the middle of a group of separate individuals; surrounded by them. There was a traitor amongst them. 2. Shared out or distributed to the members of a group. The prize was divided amongst the four finalists.
examples: There was a traitor amongst them.
The prize was divided amongst the four finalists.
Amongst the papers she found a letter dated 1912.
He was happiest amongst strangers.
Rumors spread amongst the crew within the hour.
Amongst other things, the report faults the maintenance schedule.
The residue of the estate was split amongst the surviving cousins.

entries.register: archaic; alive in American English inside one fixed phrase only
entries.complement: two coordinated noun phrases joined by and, or one plural noun phrase — never a clause, never a gerund. In the fixed phrase betwixt and between it takes no object at all and is no longer a preposition.
entries.pattern: betwixt [noun phrase] and [noun phrase] · betwixt [plural noun phrase] · betwixt and between (fixed adverbial, objectless)
entries.contrast: The archaic twin of between, from the same root as two and twin, and nothing separates them but age. The single place it is still ordinary American English is betwixt and between, meaning "neither one thing nor the other, undecided" — and there it has stopped governing anything. Its clipped poetic form is 'twixt.
variants: 'twixt — the clipped poetic form
between — the ordinary modern word
betwixt and between — the one live American survival
entries.meaning: Where you meet it: Shakespeare, the King James Bible ("that there be no strife betwixt me and thee"), hymnody, and mock-antique prose. A modern American who writes betwixt is quoting or joking, with the one exception of the fixed phrase. 1. Between — the archaic preposition, in all the senses of between. There was little love betwixt the two brothers. 2. In the fixed objectless phrase betwixt and between: neither one thing nor the other; undecided. He is betwixt and between.
examples: There was little love betwixt the two brothers.
Let there be no strife betwixt thee and me.
The cabin sat betwixt the river and the ridge.
Nothing ever came betwixt him and his work.
He is betwixt and between — too old for the draft, too young for the pension.
She has been betwixt and between about the move since February.

entries.register: archaic and regional — Scots and northern English; effectively unknown in America
entries.complement: noun phrase — never a clause, never a gerund. In the "moreover" sense it stands alone as an adverb with no object, usually at the end of the clause.
entries.pattern: forby [noun phrase] · [clause], and [noun phrase] forby. (adverbial)
entries.contrast: The two senses split cleanly and were taken over by two different English words: "besides, in addition to" went to besides and in addition to, while the older spatial "past, close by" went to past and by. Having lost both jobs, forby had nothing left to do. And do not let the modern heir be confused with its own near-twin: beside is spatial, "at the side of," while besides is additive, "in addition to" — she sat beside him against nobody besides him showed up.
variants: forbye — the commoner Scots spelling
forbys in some northern texts
entries.meaning: Where you meet it: Burns, Scott, Stevenson, Hogg, and Hardy. That is the whole list. It is here for completeness, not because any American will ever need to write it. 1. Besides; in addition to. He kept a dozen sheep, forby the cattle. 2. Past; alongside — the older spatial sense. She walked forby the kirkyard without looking in.
examples: He kept a dozen sheep, forby the cattle.
There were six of us at table, forby the children.
Forby the rent, there was coal to be paid for.
She walked forby the kirkyard without once looking in.
The road runs forby the mill and over the burn.
He is a good enough fiddler, and a joiner forby.

entries.register: poetic and archaic; it exists to save a syllable
entries.complement: noun phrase or a pronoun in the objective case — never a clause, never a gerund. Identical to against in every respect except length, and like against it is a preposition only: it has none of the adverbial use that o'er keeps, so it can never stand without an object.
entries.pattern: 'gainst [noun phrase] — in verse, wherever the meter wants one syllable where against would give two.
entries.contrast: Not a separate word at all: a metrical contraction of against, the first syllable elided and the apostrophe marking the loss. Set it beside its companions in the same trick — 'twixt, o'er, 'neath, and e'er for ever. The dialect spelling agin (I'm agin it) is a different thing: it records a pronunciation of the full word, not a contraction, and belongs to rural American speech rather than to poetry.
variants: gainst without the apostrophe in older printings
agin is the dialectal respelling of full against, not a contraction
entries.meaning: Where you meet it: Shakespeare, Milton, Keats, the metrical psalms, and the hymnbook. Anywhere a line had to scan and against was one syllable too long.
examples: He set his shoulder 'gainst the door.
The rain beat 'gainst the pane the whole night through.
Sworn 'gainst his own kin, he would not speak.
'Gainst such odds no army could have held the field.
She leaned 'gainst the gate and waited for the light.
They marched 'gainst wind and weather to the shore.

entries.register: archaic; dead in every register of modern American English
entries.complement: noun phrase — never a clause, never a gerund. It cannot be strengthened by of: ✗ maugre of his pride.
entries.pattern: Maugre [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] maugre [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: It means what despite and in spite of mean, and it lost to both. What it had that they lack is contempt: the literal sense is "in the ill will of, in defiance of," so maugre all thy pride is not a neutral concession but a taunt. Compare notwithstanding, the one concessive of this vintage that survived, and survived by moving into law.
variants: mauger, maulgre, malgre in older texts
modern French malgré is the same word
entries.meaning: Where you meet it: Chaucer, Spenser's Faerie Queene, and Shakespeare — Olivia in Twelfth Night declares her love "maugre all thy pride." Nineteenth-century antiquarians revived it for a decade or two, and then it stopped for good.
examples: Maugre all his boasting, the man never once left the harbor.
She loved him, maugre her father's rage.
Maugre the storm, the fleet stood out to sea.
He held the pass maugre every assault they made on it.
Maugre his years, the old knight rode first into the field.
I will have my say, maugre the whole council.

entries.type: simple as a preposition; a noun in its ordinary modern use
entries.register: poetic as a preposition; the noun inside *in the midst of* is ordinary formal English
entries.complement: as a preposition, a noun phrase — never a clause, never a gerund. Note carefully that in the far commoner phrase in the midst of, midst is a noun, and in and of are the prepositions doing the work.
entries.pattern: midst [noun phrase] (poetic) · in the midst of [noun phrase] (the ordinary construction) · in our / their midst
entries.contrast: The bare preposition midst belongs to verse; prose uses in the midst of, a complex preposition built on the noun and parallel to in the middle of. Against amidst and amid, its longer relatives — same root, same sense, different register. The shortest member of the family is bare poetic mid (mid the roses), which no one has written seriously in a century.
variants: 'midst — the commoner poetic spelling
mid — the shortest poetic form
amid and amidst — the prose forms
in the midst of — where midst is a noun
entries.meaning: Where you meet it: hymns, the Book of Common Prayer ("In the midst of life we are in death"), nineteenth-century verse, and the still-current phrase a traitor in our midst, in which it is a noun. 1. Poetic preposition: in the middle of; amid. Midst the din no one heard the bell. 2. Noun, inside in the midst of and in our midst — where the prepositional work is done by in and of, not by this word. There is a traitor in our midst.
examples: Midst the din no one heard the bell.
He stood 'midst the ruins of his own house.
A stranger appeared 'midst the dancers and was gone again.
There is a traitor in our midst.
In the midst of life we are in death.
She resigned in the midst of the investigation.

entries.register: poetic and archaic — hymnbooks, nineteenth-century verse, and old college songs
entries.complement: noun phrase — never a clause, never a gerund. It must have an object: unlike o'er, it kept none of the adverbial use of its parent, so ✗ the valley lay 'neath is not English.
entries.pattern: 'neath [noun phrase] — in verse, wherever the meter wants one syllable where beneath would give two.
entries.contrast: A metrical clipping of beneath, exactly as 'gainst is of against and o'er is of over. Modern prose uses under, beneath, or below. The place an American is likeliest to run into it is a hymn ("'Neath the shadow of Thy throne") or an alma mater written in the 1890s, when the college-song idiom was stiff with these forms.
variants: 'neath with the apostrophe is the standard spelling
neath without it appears in later printings
beneath is the full form
entries.meaning: Nothing but a shorter beneath. It has no meaning of its own, only a syllable count, and that is the entire reason it exists.
examples: 'Neath the shadow of the elms we sang the old songs.
He sleeps 'neath the sod of his own field.
The valley lay 'neath a sheet of cloud all morning.
'Neath her window he waited until dawn.
Buried 'neath the church floor, the founder rests there still.
The colors passed 'neath the arch to the sound of drums.

entries.register: poetic and archaic — and yet every American hears it several times a year
entries.complement: noun phrase — never a clause, never a gerund. Like over, it can also be an adverb with no object at all (the battle o'er), and in verse that objectless use is often postposed.
entries.pattern: o'er [noun phrase] · [noun phrase] o'er (adverbial, postposed in verse)
entries.contrast: Nothing but a one-syllable over. Where over would give a poet two syllables and the line needs one, o'er appears. Its family is the whole set of poetic elisions — e'er for ever, ne'er for never, heav'n, ev'ry — and the compound o'erhead. It has no separate meaning whatever, and treating it as more solemn than over is a misreading.
variants: oer without the apostrophe in some older printings
o'erhead, o'ercome, o'erthrow in verse compounds
entries.meaning: Where you meet it: "O'er the ramparts we watched" and "O'er the land of the free" — the national anthem alone keeps this word in the ear of the entire country, which makes it the one archaic preposition every American knows without knowing it. Beyond that, hymns, Poe, Longfellow, and the metrical Psalms. 1. Above or across — the spatial senses of over, and the ones the anthem uses. O'er the ramparts we watched. 2. Throughout; all over — of sound, light, or anything that spreads across a whole area. The bells rang out o'er the sleeping town. 3. Adverb, with no object at all: over, finished — often postposed in verse. The battle o'er, they buried their dead.
examples: O'er the ramparts we watched, were so gallantly streaming.
The banner yet waves o'er the land of the free.
He wandered lonely o'er the hills that summer.
A shadow passed o'er her face and was gone.
The bells rang out o'er the sleeping town.
O'er moor and fen, o'er crag and torrent, lead thou me on.
The battle o'er, the field was left to the crows.
The long night at last was o'er.
Word of the surrender spread o'er the whole county before nightfall.

entries.register: archaic; extinct since about 1650
entries.complement: as a preposition, a noun phrase naming a time (sith that day). It was far commoner as a conjunction taking a full finite clause (sith you will not hear me), and nearly every surviving example is of that kind. It never takes a gerund.
entries.pattern: sith [noun phrase] (preposition) · sith [clause] (conjunction — the usual case)
entries.contrast: The ancestor of since, which absorbed both of its jobs — the temporal "from that time onward" and the causal "seeing that" — and drove it out by about 1650. It has no connection whatever to the Sith of Star Wars, an invented name, though that is now the only place most Americans have seen the letters in that order.
variants: sithence, sithen, sithens in Middle and early Modern English
since is the modern reflex
entries.meaning: Where you meet it: Shakespeare — Claudius asks the courtiers to stay "sith nor th'exterior nor the inward man resembles that it was" — together with Spenser, Sidney, and the Elizabethan sonneteers.
